sources.title: Maṇimēkalai · English translation by Kausalya Hart
sources.edition: Project Madurai Unicode text; English translation by Kausalya Hart

claims.subject: tamil_chitrapathi
claims.summary: Chitrāpathi is identified as Mādhavi’s mother.
claims.speaker: narrator
claims.note: Source-local relationship in this epic; no identity is inferred with similarly named figures elsewhere.

claims.subject: tamil_madhavi
claims.summary: Mādhavi refers to Manimekalai as her daughter.
claims.speaker: Mādhavi, in the narrative reported by Aravanar
claims.note: The canto passage identifies Mādhavi as Chitrāpathi’s daughter and says that Manimekalai is her daughter. This is a textual kinship claim.

claims.subject: tamil_ettikumaran
claims.summary: Ettikumaran is identified as the prince Udayakumaran’s friend.
claims.speaker: narrator
claims.note: This is the Chola prince in Maṇimēkalai. Do not merge automatically with other similarly named Udaya figures.

claims.subject: tamil_udayakumaran
claims.summary: Udayakumaran tells Ettikumaran that he intends to bring Manimekalai to him, and the narrative describes his attraction to her.
claims.speaker: Udayakumaran and narrator
claims.note: This records the epic’s courtship plot, not a historical relationship.

search_log.outcome: Inspected the English translation text and prologue summary. Canto 2 passages identify the kinship and friendship claims; retained source-local names and did not merge them with similarly named epic or puranic figures.

search_log.outcome: Identified potential scaling sources (SARIT TEI corpus, GRETIL plain-text editions, Project Madurai Unicode texts). Only Project Madurai’s inspected page explicitly grants redistribution subject to retaining its header; terms must be checked per collection and edition before bulk reuse.

notes: Accuracy-over-volume addition: five Maṇimēkalai individuals and passage-level relationships, all within the work’s own narrative frame. Do not treat these names as independently historical or merge them across texts without separate identity evidence.

Scale-up corpus/index candidates: SARIT (Sanskrit and Buddhist text corpus with TEI/XML-oriented editions and metadata); GRETIL (machine-readable electronic Sanskrit texts, generally plain-text editions); Muktabodha Digital Library (Sanskrit source texts, with work-specific access/reuse terms); Tamil Virtual Academy and the Central Institute of Classical Tamil digital library/catalogues for Tamil texts. Their text and license coverage varies by individual text/edition; catalog presence is not a blanket reuse license.

Project Madurai is a particularly practical Tamil source: the inspected Maṇimēkalai page states that the file may be freely distributed provided its header is retained, and acknowledges permission for inclusion. Preserve that header and attribution in any derived corpus; verify each file independently.

Scaling toward 3,000 should begin with an inventory keyed by work/edition/language, stable passage identifiers, machine-readable format, access method, and explicit reuse status. Use transliteration/normalization only as an index aid, retain original passage and edition locators, and route all candidate entities through source-local identity review before linking across works.
